rules.title: RSA Digital Signature Vulnerable to Shor's Algorithm
rules.rationale: Shor's algorithm computes integer prime factors in polynomial time on a Cryptanalytically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC), breaking the mathematical assumption underlying RSA signature authenticity.
rules.quantum_relevance: Directly vulnerable to polynomial-time forgery via Shor's algorithm once a CRQC is realized.

recommendation.action: Initiate quantum migration planning to transition public-key digital signatures to NIST-standardized Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) signature algorithms.
recommendation.reason: RSA signatures cannot withstand quantum cryptanalysis. Systems must migrate before long-lived certificates, trust anchors, or signed binaries outlive the CRQC horizon.

rules.title: ECDSA Signature Vulnerable to Shor's Algorithm
rules.rationale: Shor's algorithm solves elliptic-curve discrete logarithms in polynomial time, completely compromising ECDSA private keys and enabling signature forgery.
rules.quantum_relevance: Directly vulnerable via Shor's algorithm. All standard curves (NIST P-256, P-384, secp256k1) are broken.

recommendation.action: Transition to post-quantum signature schemes (NIST FIPS 204 ML-DSA or FIPS 205 SLH-DSA) or hybrid classical-quantum signatures.
recommendation.reason: ECDSA provides zero security against quantum adversaries capable of running Shor's algorithm.

rules.title: Ed25519 Signature Vulnerable to Shor's Algorithm
rules.rationale: Ed25519 (EdDSA over Curve25519) relies on the discrete logarithm problem over elliptic curves, which is solvable in polynomial time by Shor's algorithm.
rules.quantum_relevance: Directly vulnerable to private key recovery and signature forgery via Shor's algorithm.

recommendation.action: Plan migration to stateful hash-based signatures for firmware or lattice-based ML-DSA for interactive protocols.
recommendation.reason: Elliptic curve cryptography provides no defense against Shor's algorithm regardless of implementation robustness.

rules.title: ECDH Key Establishment Vulnerable to Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL)
rules.rationale: Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm. Adversaries can record encrypted ciphertext today and decrypt it retrospectively when a CRQC becomes operational (Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later).
rules.quantum_relevance: Subject to immediate Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL) risk for any data whose confidentiality lifetime exceeds the CRQC horizon.

recommendation.action: Deploy hybrid post-quantum key encapsulation mechanisms (KEM) combining classical ECDH with ML-KEM (Kyber) or pure ML-KEM.
recommendation.reason: Traffic captured today can be stored by adversaries and decrypted later. Long-lived confidential data requires immediate hybrid or post-quantum key encapsulation.

rules.title: Finite-Field Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange Vulnerable to HNDL
rules.rationale: Finite-field Diffie-Hellman (FFDHE) relies on the discrete logarithm problem in multiplicative groups of integers modulo a prime, which Shor's algorithm solves efficiently.
rules.quantum_relevance: Vulnerable to retrospective decryption under Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later threat models.

recommendation.action: Replace finite-field Diffie-Hellman with hybrid KEMs (e.g., X25519 + ML-KEM-768) or pure ML-KEM-768.
recommendation.reason: Classical key exchange offers zero confidentiality protection against future quantum decryption of recorded traffic.

rules.title: AES-128 Effective Security Halved by Grover's Algorithm
rules.rationale: Grover's search algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for brute-force key search, reducing the effective security of AES-128 from 128 bits to approximately 64 bits.
rules.quantum_relevance: Grover's algorithm provides a square-root speedup ($O(\sqrt{N})$), making 128-bit symmetric keys borderline for ultra-high-assurance or classified workloads.

recommendation.action: Upgrade symmetric encryption from AES-128 to AES-256 for long-term confidentiality.
recommendation.reason: AES-256 maintains a comfortable 128-bit quantum security margin against Grover's algorithm, satisfying post-quantum security requirements (e.g., NSA CNSA 2.0).

rules.title: AES-256 Symmetric Cipher is Quantum-Resistant
rules.rationale: AES-256 provides 256 bits of classical security and 128 bits of post-quantum security against Grover's algorithm, which exceeds all foreseeable quantum computational brute-force bounds.
rules.quantum_relevance: Quantum-resistant. Grover's algorithm reduces 256 bits to 128 bits of security, which is computationally infeasible to break.

recommendation.action: Retain AES-256 as the symmetric encryption standard; ensure it is deployed in AEAD modes (such as GCM).
recommendation.reason: AES-256 meets NIST and NSA CNSA 2.0 requirements for post-quantum symmetric confidentiality.

rules.title: Fast Hash Function (SHA-256) Inappropriately Used for Password Storage
rules.rationale: SHA-256 is an unkeyed general-purpose cryptographic hash function engineered for rapid computation. It lacks memory-hardness and work factor controls, enabling adversaries to execute billions of guesses per second on consumer GPUs.
rules.quantum_relevance: Conventional security vulnerability, NOT a quantum risk. Grover's algorithm is irrelevant; classical offline cracking tools (hashcat, John the Ripper) break unsalted or fast hashes effortlessly today.

recommendation.action: Replace SHA-256 password storage immediately with a standardized, memory-hard password-hashing function such as Argon2id, bcrypt, or scrypt.
recommendation.reason: Password storage requires computational and memory hardness to defend against offline GPU/ASIC brute-force dictionary attacks. Post-quantum algorithms do not solve this problem.

rules.title: Cryptographically Broken Hash Function MD5 in Active Use
rules.rationale: MD5 suffers from catastrophic collision vulnerabilities, allowing practical chosen-prefix collision attacks in seconds on commodity hardware.
rules.quantum_relevance: Classical cryptanalytic failure, not a quantum issue. MD5 was broken classically in 2004.

recommendation.action: Migrate from MD5 to SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-3 for integrity checks and signatures.
recommendation.reason: MD5 provides zero collision resistance. Attackers can forge valid certificates, signatures, or checksums.

rules.title: Deprecated and Collision-Vulnerable Hash Function SHA-1 in Use
rules.rationale: SHA-1 has practical collision vulnerabilities (SHAttered, Shambles attacks) and has been formally deprecated by NIST (NIST SP 800-131A) and major web browsers.
rules.quantum_relevance: Classical collision vulnerability. This is a conventional hygiene issue, not a post-quantum migration issue.

recommendation.action: Replace SHA-1 with modern hash algorithms such as SHA-256 or SHA-3.
recommendation.reason: SHA-1 collisions allow attackers to produce colliding documents or certificates with identical signatures.

rules.title: Legacy 64-Bit Block Cipher (DES / 3DES) in Use
rules.rationale: DES and Triple-DES use an obsolete 64-bit block size, rendering them vulnerable to birthday collision attacks (Sweet32) in TLS and bulk encryption, alongside small key size limitations.
rules.quantum_relevance: Classical block cipher vulnerability. Deprecated by NIST SP 800-131A Rev 2 since 2023.

recommendation.action: Decommission DES/3DES immediately and migrate to AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305.
recommendation.reason: 64-bit block ciphers leak plaintext after approximately 32 GB of data under the same key (Sweet32 attack).

rules.title: Insecure Stream Cipher RC4 in Use
rules.rationale: RC4 has multiple severe statistical biases in its keystream output (RC4 NOMORE attack), allowing practical plaintext recovery in TLS sessions.
rules.quantum_relevance: Classical keystream bias vulnerability. Formally prohibited in TLS by RFC 7465.

recommendation.action: Disable RC4 across all cipher suites and migrate to modern authenticated ciphers.
recommendation.reason: RC4 is completely insecure against passive classical eavesdroppers.

rules.title: Insecure Electronic Codebook (ECB) Cipher Mode
rules.rationale: Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode encrypts identical plaintext blocks into identical ciphertext blocks, preserving structural patterns and failing semantic security.
rules.quantum_relevance: Mode of operation architectural failure, not a quantum issue.

recommendation.action: Switch from ECB mode to an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) mode such as GCM or CCM.
recommendation.reason: ECB mode leaks data confidentiality through structural pattern visibility and provides no message integrity.

rules.title: Sub-2048 Bit RSA Key Vulnerable to Classical Factoring
rules.rationale: RSA keys smaller than 2048 bits (e.g., 512, 1024 bits) can be factored using classical General Number Field Sieve (GNFS) algorithms on academic or cloud compute resources.
rules.quantum_relevance: Vulnerable to classical computers today, irrespective of future quantum advancements.

recommendation.action: Immediately revoke and replace sub-2048 bit RSA keys with at least RSA-2048/3072 or transition directly to PQC signatures.
recommendation.reason: RSA-1024 was deprecated by NIST in 2013 and offers insufficient resistance against classical factoring clusters.
